extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of political theology, theologians, civil sovereigns and subjects interested in obedience, salvation, and ecclesiastical authority
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles about when to obey God versus civil sovereigns, what is necessary for salvation (faith and obedience), and how to interpret/scripturally justify ecclesiastical and civil authority. Focused guidance on the limits of pastoral power, sources of faith, and criteria for doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority when commands conflict: obey God if known
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man receiveth two contrary Commands, and knows that one of them is God's, he ought to obey that, and not the other, though it be the command even of his lawful Sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a command can be identified as from God, obedience to God supersedes obedience to any civil authority; the practical difficulty lies in discerning whether a command truly comes from God (false prophets and false teachers make this uncertain). Beware of persons who abuse God's name for private ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish what is necessary to salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who can distinguish between what is Necessary, and what is not Necessary for their Reception into the Kingdome of God, need not be troubled by conflicts of obedience between God and the civil sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sovereign's command can be obeyed without forfeiture of eternal life, failure to obey is unjust; if obeying it would lead to eternal damnation, one must disobey. Therefore citizens must be taught to distinguish necessary from non-necessary matters for salvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two essentials for salvation: Faith and Obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: All that is NECESSARY to Salvation, is contained in two Vertues, Faith in Christ, and Obedience to Laws. The latter (if perfect) would suffice, but because of sin a Remission of sins (reward of Faith) is also required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obedience is the willing endeavour to obey (also called Charity, Love, Righteousness, Repentance). Faith provides remission of past sins. Together they make up what is required for reception into the Kingdom of God.

rubrics_metrics.name: The only necessary article of faith: 'Jesus is the Christ' (Unum Necessarium)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onely Necessary Article Of Christian Faith ... is this, that JESUS IS THE CHRIST. By 'Christ' is meant the King promised by the prophets who gives eternal life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes offers multiple arguments that this single article is sufficient: the scope of the Evangelists, the subject of the Apostles' sermons, the easiness of the doctrine (e.g., the thief on the cross), clear scriptural texts (e.g., John 20:31), and its role as the foundation of other articles. Many other doctrines are either deducible from this or implicit consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as necessary faith beyond the foundation article
rubrics_metrics.description: Other articles (e.g., God's omnipotence, resurrection) are necessary only insofar as they are contained in or deducible from the foundational belief that Jesus is the Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a believer holds the foundational article, he implicitly holds or is entitled to hold all consequences derivable from it even if he cannot articulate them; hence explicit assent to every disputed doctrine is not required for salvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and sufficiency of Obedience (repentance/will)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Obedience required by God accepts the Will for the Deed and is a serious Endeavour to Obey him; called Charity, Love, Righteousness, or Repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: God may accept the will and endeavour as equivalent to the deed; therefore sincere desire and turning from sin (repentance) constitutes the obedience necessary for salvation even where perfect performance is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of God are the Laws of Nature and the civil laws of sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The Laws of God therefore are none but the Laws of Nature, whereof the principal is that we should not violate our Faith, that is, a command to obey our Civil Sovereigns, constituted by mutual pact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christ gave counsel to observe the laws one is subject to (laws of nature and laws of sovereigns); he did not enact a new civil law-code. Thus obedience to lawful civil authority typically counts as obedience to God when it does not demand forfeiture of eternal life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith ordinarily comes by hearing lawful pastors; authority to examine doctrines lies with the Supreme Pastor
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith cometh by Hearing — by Hearing our lawful Pastors. The ordinary cause of believing the Scriptures is the teaching of those allowed and appointed to teach (parents, pastors). Examination of doctrines belongs to the Supreme Pastor (civil sovereign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The social process (teachers' reputation and office) is primary in forming belief. While 1 John advises testing spirits, in practice Christians who lack special revelation rely on their pastors and the authority established by the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret Scripture by the scope and harmony of the writer, not isolated texts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the bare Words, but the Scope of the writer that giveth the true light, by which any writing is to be interpreted; those that insist upon single Texts, without considering the main Design, can derive nothing clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid atomizing scripture (picking single verses) and instead consider plain, uncontroverted passages in light of the whole Scripture's purpose; this reduces misinterpretation and manipulation of texts for private advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of pastoral/pope power: teaching vs coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Power to Teach is distinct from a Coercive Power in the Pope over Kings. Christ gave the power/command to teach, but refused worldly coercion and advised letting good and evil grow together until Judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastoral authority includes teaching and admonishing; it does not include deposing kings, killing heretics, or enforcing spiritual sentences by temporal force. Historical acts of excommunication or coercion are not authoritative proofs of rightful papal temporal power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical examples do not establish ecclesiastical right
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples prove nothing; the Examples alleged (Jehoiada, Ambrose, Gregory I, Zachary, Leo III) do not make probable a right of the Pope to coercive temporal power and many acts cited are crimes or void as given in their own cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer legitimate ecclesiastical jurisdiction or temporal authority merely from historical incidents; such acts may have been unlawful, exceptional, or self-interested rather than normative precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the civil sovereign is infidel: external obedience, internal faith preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Civil Sovereign is an Infidel, every one of his own Subjects that resisteth him sinneth against the Laws of God (laws of nature) and rejecteth apostolic counsel to obey princes; faith remains internal and invisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects must obey outwardly and keep their faith inwardly; they should not make war on the infidel sovereign. If they suffer for their faith, they may expect reward in heaven, but seeking martyrdom or rebellion is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: How Faith and Works jointly justify (senses of 'justify')
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith and Obedience are both necessary to Salvation; 'Justification by Works' should be understood as the Will or Endeavour (which God may accept), while 'Justification by Faith' denotes that faith makes the plea acceptable to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish senses: (a) justification as being 'denominated just' because of will/endeavour; (b) justification as acceptance of an insufficient plea because faith makes it acceptable. Both language-meanings justify the claim that faith and obedience operate together.
